content: Radical surgery has been the standard treatment for early-stage vulvar cancer since the mid-20th century. While survival rates have been excellent, the procedure is associated with a high rate of complications. Since the 1980s, surgical approaches have been tailored to individual patients in an effort to reduce these complications, particularly in those with limited disease. The objective of this analysis was to compare the effectiveness and safety of individualized surgical treatments with those of traditional, more extensive surgical procedures. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to April 2007. Additional sources, such as hand-searched journals, reference lists, gynecological cancer handbooks, and conference abstracts, were also reviewed. The studies included in this analysis focused on patients with cT1N0M0 squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. The outcomes assessed were overall survival, disease-specific survival, disease-free survival (DFS), treatment-related complications, and quality of life (QoL). The data were independently reviewed and extracted by three authors to ensure accuracy and reliability. The findings from three studies revealed no significant difference in the rate of local vulvar cancer recurrence between radical local excision and radical vulvectomy. Similarly, there was no difference in groin recurrence rates between ipsilateral groin node dissection and bilateral groin node dissection in patients with well-lateralized tumors. However, superficial groin node dissection was found to be less safe compared to full femoro-inguinal lymph node dissection. The triple incision technique was determined to be a safe surgical option, provided that tumor-free margins were greater than 8 mm. Although this technique was associated with a slight increase in recurrence rates, the reduction in complications made it a viable alternative. On the other hand, omitting femoral lymph node dissection led to a higher incidence of groin recurrences, indicating that this step remains critical in certain cases. The authors concluded that the current evidence on surgical management for early vulvar cancer is of generally low quality. However, based on the available data, radical local excision appears to be a safe alternative to radical vulvectomy for early-stage disease. In patients with lateralized tumors, contralateral groin node dissection can be omitted. Additionally, the triple incision technique is as safe as en bloc dissection, provided adequate tumor-free margins are achieved. Despite these findings, the omission of femoral lymph node dissection increases the risk of groin recurrences. The authors emphasized the need for higher-quality studies to provide more reliable evidence. However, conducting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in this field may be challenging due to the rarity of vulvar cancer. As an alternative, well-designed observational studies could offer valuable insights into optimizing surgical management for this condition.
